problem: Transformer-based end-to-end navigation models have fixed context windows, and even linear-attention models with unbounded memory are trained statelessly (memory reset to zero each batch), so they never learn to exploit long-horizon persistent memory or adapt online within one environment.
motivation: Real robots operate continuously in the same environment, so long-term memory for sustained adaptation is essential. The authors argue the bottleneck is the training protocol, not the architecture: zero-initialized memory during training mismatches the long evolving memory states seen at deployment.
key_idea: Train a linear-attention (RWKV-7) navigation policy statefully by carrying the recurrent memory state from the end of one training batch to the start of the next, approximating training on an infinite interaction stream.
insight: The same architecture and parameter count trained statefully beats the stateless version (ProcTHOR SR 0.580 vs 0.420) and a fixed-window Transformer. The stateful model's success rate keeps rising as context length grows, while the stateless model plateaus or degrades, which the authors read as emergent in-context learning. Memory-norm RSD is lower under stateful training, consistent with training under an approximately stationary memory-state distribution.
method: Stateful training: the final memory state of batch b initializes batch b+1 (M_T^(b) -> M_0^(b+1)); gradients are truncated within each batch, and the loss is per-batch imitation NLL
Linear-attention action decoder: RWKV-7 with 18 layers, hidden size 512, ~0.2B parameters, replacing the SPOC Transformer decoder; a fixed-size memory gives constant per-step cost

Goal-conditioned encoders: frozen SigLIP encodes the text goal and the navigation and manipulation camera images, and a SPOC-style visual encoder fuses them into o_t; goal cross-attention is removed so multiple instructions can occur in one trajectory
Continual Object Navigation (CON) benchmark: an unbounded goal sequence in one persistent environment, goals revealed only after the previous one is completed, with repeats allowed
Data: procedurally generated Maze (15x15 grid, 1k envs, 50K trajectories of length 2000, 100M steps) and ProcTHOR (1k envs, 5K trajectories, 10M steps)
Optimization view: stateless training optimizes under M_0=0, while stateful training samples memory states from the model's own induced (approximately stationary) distribution d_theta

setting.backbone: RWKV-7 linear attention decoder (18 layers, dim 512) with frozen SigLIP encoders and a SPOC-style visual encoder, trained from scratch by imitation
setting.training_data: Imitation on expert trajectories in procedurally generated environments: ProcTHOR 10M frames (5K trajectories x 2000 steps), Maze 10M-frame training (the dataset table lists 100M steps)
setting.observation: egocentric RGB from navigation and manipulation cameras (394x224 in ProcTHOR) plus a text goal; a partially observed grid view in Maze
setting.action_space: discrete low-level navigation actions (softmax over actions)
setting.simulator: AI2-THOR (ProcTHOR) and a custom grid Maze

numbers.eval_set_note: 16 unseen test environments, 5000 steps each, 1000 steps per instruction

numbers_note: The ICL-vs-context-length and memory RSD results appear only in figures. Success rate is printed as a 0-1 fraction, which is kept as printed. The paper does not print 0-100 percentages.
results: On CON in ProcTHOR, stateful StateLinFormer reaches SR 0.580 and 496 steps to goal, vs 0.420 stateless and 0.479 for SPOC-10M. It also slightly beats SPOC-Pretrained (0.566, trained on 40M frames). In Maze, SR is 0.77 vs 0.64 stateless and 0.68 for SPOC-10M.
limitations: No formal convergence or stability guarantee for the induced memory-state distribution
Evaluated only on synthetic procedural navigation (Maze, ProcTHOR) with a small test set of 16 environments; no real-robot or standard benchmark results, and other domains are untested
Baselines are limited to SPOC (Transformer, context reset per task), and the ICL claim relies on a single figure
